blocks.content: The Post-Gupta Period marks the transition from the classical age of the Guptas to the early medieval period of Indian history. After the decline of the Gupta Empire in the mid- 6th century AD, India witnessed political fragmentation, the rise of regional kingdoms, foreign invasions, and significant socio-economic changes. Despite political instability, this period laid the foundation for early medieval India.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Harshavardhana belonged to the Pushyabhuti dynasty and shifted his capital from Thanesar to Kannauj.
Court poet Banabhatta authored the biography Harshacharita and the famous romance novel Kadambari.
Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) visited India during Harsha's rule and documented socio-economic and religious conditions in Si-Yu-Ki.
Harsha's southward imperial expansion was successfully repelled at the Narmada River by Chalukya King Pulakeshin II.
Harsha patronized Buddhism and authored three celebrated Sanskrit plays: Ratnavali, Priyadarsika, and Nagananda.

blocks.content: The decline of the Gupta Empire was not due to a single factor but a combination of political, military, economic, and administrative reasons.

cells: Repeated invasions by Hunas weakened Gupta military power
Later Gupta rulers lacked ability and authority
Decline in trade and reduction in gold coinage
Loss of revenue due to grants to officials and religious institutions

blocks.content: After the fall of the Guptas, northern India was divided among several small kingdoms. Prominent among them were the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, Maukharis of Kannauj, Maitrakas of Vallabhi, and later the Vardhana dynasty under Harshavardhana.
Harshavardhana emerged as the most powerful ruler of North India after the Guptas. He belonged to the Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty and ruled from 606 AD to 647 AD.
Harsha was born in 590 AD. His father was Prabhakaravardhana, the ruler of Thanesar. After the death of his father and brother Rajyavardhana, Harsha ascended the throne at a very young age.
Harsha carried out extensive military campaigns to consolidate his empire. He conquered Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Bengal, and parts of central India.
Harsha attempted to expand into the Deccan but was defeated by the Chalukya ruler Pulakesin II on the banks of the Narmada River. This defeat marked the southern
Harshavardhana united the kingdoms of Thanesar and Kannauj, marking the last great imperial consolidation in Northern India prior to the medieval period.
boundary of Harsha’s empire.
Harsha followed the Gupta administrative system with modifications. The empire was divided into provinces, districts, and villages.
The king was the supreme authority. Officials included Mahasamantas, Kumaramatyas, and Sandhivigrahika.
Village assemblies played an important role. Land grants became common during this period.

rows: Advance south of Narmada was checked
Successfully defended northern frontier and took title 'Parameshvara'

blocks.content: Agriculture was the main source of income. Trade declined compared to the Gupta period, and gold coinage became rare.
The caste system became rigid. Untouchability increased. The position of women declined, and practices like sati were reported.
Harsha was initially a Shaivite but later became a patron of Mahayana Buddhism. He was tolerant towards all religions.
Harsha organized religious assemblies at Prayag, where donations were distributed to monks, scholars, and the poor.
Nalanda University flourished during this period. Harsha himself was a great scholar and playwright.
Harsha authored three Sanskrit plays: Ratnavali, Nagananda, and Priyadarshika.

items: The Aihole Inscription, composed in Sanskrit by court poet Ravikirti, records Pulakeshin II's victory over Harshavardhana.
Match-the-following questions often test Harsha's literary works: Ratnavali, Priyadarsika, and Nagananda.
Harsha organized the grand religious assembly at Kannauj and the quinquennial almsgiving event called Mahamoksha Parishad at Prayag.

blocks.content: The Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang visited India during Harsha’s reign. His account provides valuable information about administration, society, religion, and education.
Art declined compared to the Gupta period, but Buddhist monasteries and stupas continued to be built.
Harsha died without an heir in 647 AD. After his death, his empire disintegrated rapidly, leading to political instability in northern India.
Harsha’s reign represents the last great empire of ancient India. It acted as a bridge between ancient and early medieval India.
